title: Potential and Limitations of the Electronic Medication List (eML) as a Tool for Medication Safety
summary:
To ensure safe medication therapy, it is important to have an up-to-date and complete overview of all medications being taken. In the healthcare system, however, such information is often stored in different locations - for example, with primary care physicians and specialists, at pharmacies, at long-term care facilities or with the patients themselves. This information may differ from one source to another or be incomplete. As a result, for example, medications may be prescribed twice, interactions may be overlooked, or medications that are no longer needed may continue to be taken.
The automatically generated electronic medication list in the electronic health record is intended to clearly consolidate the prescribed medications from various healthcare facilities. However, it is not yet sufficiently known how complete and up-to-date this list is compared to the medications actually being taken.
This study examines how accurately the electronic medication list and information from primary care physicians reflect the medications actually taken and to what extent they align with medication records from various physicians, pharmacies and other healthcare providers involved in patient care. The aim is to determine how frequently discrepancies occur, what types of discrepancies exist and what possible causes underlie them.
The study does not evaluate whether a treatment is medically appropriate but rather focuses exclusively on whether the various medication records match.
The study consists of two parts and is conducted at a primary care practice. In the first part, existing routine data from 350 adult patients with public health insurance are retrospectively analyzed. 
In the second part, 135 adult patients with public health insurance participate in a one-time interview after providing written consent. They bring all medications taken regularly or as needed, as well as any other preparations they use, so that these can be recorded together. In addition, the patient’s personal medication plan, available medication records from other treating facilities and the electronic medication list are compiled and compared with one another.
conditions: (In)completeness or contradictory documentation of the medications patients are taking, which can lead to medication errors and an increased risk to medication safety

interventions.name:
Part 1: Retrospective one-time comparison of the eML and local medication data for 350 adult patients with public health insurance at a primary care practice

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Insured under a statutory health insurance scheme.
- informed consent to participate in the study.
- sufficient language proficiency and cognitive ability to participate in the data collection process (non-German-speaking individuals will not be included in the study).
- access to the eML.
- treatment at a participating primary care practice.
Exclusion criteria:
- no treatment at a participating primary care practice.
